utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. May the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, good morning. This is the case number IT-03-69-PT, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, David Re accompanied by Rachel Riedman, legal officer, and case managers Carmela Javier and Mr. Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For Mr. Stanisic, myself Wayne Jordash. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am Zoran Jovanovic, attorney from Belgrade, and I represent Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic. We had -- or our Senior Legal Officer Linda Murnane was so kind to hold a 65 ter meeting yesterday which, as I appreciate, has done a lot for the preparation of this meeting and clarified things or things were clarified in the meantime, maybe. Our last Status Conference here was in August, on the 14th of August. It was necessary to find a date for the new Status Conference within 120 days and so originally we had scheduled this meeting for next week but it turned out it was conflicting with other assignments of one of the counsel and so we rescheduled it to today. The agenda I would like to discuss would be, first, pending motions; and then disclosure issues as a second point; and then preparations for pre-trial and for trial phase; and other matters. As for the first issue of pending motions, we have to address a Defence motion on modification of conditions for provisional release of one of the accused. I would like to ask about the health of both accused and, therefore, may we here move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So the other pending motion concerns the review of the Registrar's decision pursuant to Article 13(B) of the practice direction on the assignment of counsel which was filed confidentially on the 13th of September, 2006. As was explained by the -- our Senior Legal Officer at yesterday's 65 ter conference, the Trial Chamber will be able to issue a decision in January. The Trial Chamber is very aware of the practical importance of this decision for the Stanisic Defence counsel. Regarding a further extension of the deadline for further arguments on this matter, as was explained during aforementioned 65 ter conference, the deadline for further arguments was extended during the last Status Conference and will not be extended again. May I now move to another topic, if no comment is being wished on this one. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, the Prosecution takes no view on this at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So now as to the disclosure issue. First, regarding Rule 66(A)(i) about supporting material to the indictment and, (ii), witness statements as well as Rule 68 mitigating and exculpatory material, Rule 66(B) inspection of Prosecution books, photos, and other tangible objects. I would like to say the following or to ask the following: During yesterday's 65 ter conference, the Prosecution responded that the disclosure of documents from these VRS archives to the Defence can be completed during the next month. Is that still the Prosecution's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the decision to put on the -- in the Status Conference is the Prosecution has finally gained access to the VRS archive and has been there twice and has selected a number of documents of potential relevance to this case. We have taken several hundred documents. We are currently reviewing them. Within the next month, we should be able to make a final decision as to whether or not we would use them at trial and will disclose them to the Defence by the end of December. That's the VRS archive ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then as to translations of documents, we have to clarify the following: During yesterday's 65 ter conference, the Prosecution indicated that 33 translations have been disclosed but that 20 translations were still pending; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not quite. It's actually 18. We have reviewed our records. We have 18 pending translations. I can't, unfortunately, give a date for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because they are in the translation queue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. But let's monitor that. And then yesterday also the matter of this Mijovic audio tape was apparently raised. Has the audible copy which was needed of the audio tape now been provided to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, it's now in the hands of both Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Jordash who have them with them at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you confirm that? Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution has disclosed to the Defence the CD with the interview which is technically sound now, I believe, so that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now next is the disclosure of certain letters used in the Milosevic case. This disclosure is awaiting Rule 70 permission. Does the Prosecution have an indication when that permission will arrive, as this issue has been pending for quite some time now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are two letters. We have communicated with Mr. Stanisic's lawyers. The first lawyer isn't a Rule 71 and the information is public; we've communicated that to them. The second letter which counsel for Mr. Stanisic has indicated that he has seen and is aware of the information in the Milosevic letter, several months ago we sought -- in September, we sought Rule 70 clearance from the relevant providing government. We're still awaiting that. It's always difficult to know. We can send a reminder letter but that doesn't mean it will speed things up because they have to go through government clearance processes. We are just simply asking for the same clearance that was provided to Mr. Milosevic, Slobodan Milosevic, be provided to counsel for Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic, if necessary, but I just can't give you a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Then the Prosecution has indicated that as to further matters which might arise under these rules pertaining to the duty to disclosure, there are statements currently being produced concerning testimony before the Belgrade court which are being made available to counsel on CD-ROM. Counsel for Mr. Simatovic indicated he already had this testimony. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Simatovic is following the trial and it is thanks to the Court, or, rather, the district court for war crimes in Belgrade. These transcripts are being sent on a regular basis, and the Prosecution also sent us in the transcripts from that trial that it considers to be relevant, so I think that that issue has been resolved as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We would like disclosure from the Prosecution. I know we have been following the trial to a degree, but we would like disclosure, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That makes sense, doesn't it, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I can happily report that Mr. Jovanovic now has two copies of the transcript and Mr. Jordash has one. We have provided them with -- on CD today with the entirety of the transcript that we have of the proceedings in Belgrade. Now we're obtaining this on a sporadic basis as it's updated, and we will, of course, give it to them. Now, some of that does contain statements which would be relevant under Rule 66(B) of intended Prosecution witnesses in the Trnovo component of this indictment. They are of course not translated into English, they are in their original, and that's all we can do for the moment. We have no immediate plans to translate it. But if anything is relevant, we will do so in the future, once we've identified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Re. I would now like to go to the expert reports under Rule 94 bis. Have the translations of the Strinovic exhumation reports been disclosed already? That is pending already since spring 2005, I think, isn't it? Please, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They still are -- there is a difficulty here. They were tendered in totality in the Milosevic case and they were accepted in the original B/C/S in the Milosevic case. They're basically exhumation reports. The Court granted the Prosecution some leeway in not having them translated. They are still pending. They are still in the queue but there is no priority for that. This is very much an issue which, in our submission, the Defence could look at those and decide whether they really want them translated into English for the purposes of tendering because it's something which can be stipulated because they relate to the fact of death and the circumstances, and it probably won't be an issue when it comes to the trial. So that may be an issue for further discussion, rather than having the CLSS translate things which may not need to be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I understand. What would you say? Wouldn't that be an approach possible saving resources?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It seems very reasonable to me, and we will look at them and if, as expected, there will be no dispute on them, then we can agree and save translation resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you also agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I do agree. And the Defence, in conformity with what we were discussing earlier on at the previous Status Conference and with respect to 65 ter, we are expecting the Prosecution to provide us with a proposal for adjudicated, or agreed facts, rather, and in that sense, that will be -- those will be the certificates, death certificates, and when we receive the proposal, I think it will suffice to be in English and need not be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, these were not in English but in B/C/S. Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do apologise, Your Honour. So it is agreed facts, and I think the Prosecution said that it would formulate a proposal, and in keeping with what was decided at the previous Status Conference and at the 65 ter meeting, I think that proposal incorporates these death certificates and the component parts of the expertise, that is what the Defence is expecting but we don't have to have it translated into the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. I think this would be a very good solution, on the one hand to save resources, and on the other hand, already go into the agreed facts matter which we will touch upon later in this meeting. Anything further to that translations issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just there might be a slight confusion. My understanding is the autopsy report is almost the same thing as the death certificate for the purposes of the stipulation but -- we'll certainly work on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, please. Usually these are two different documents but they are, of course, related closely. So now for further pre-trial preparation. I would like to address the following. First as to the possible use of Rule 92 bis and 89(F) evidence. How far is the Prosecution in preparing that packages, according to 89(F) and 92 ter, as this has a direct impact on the Prosecution's readiness for the trial, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As I indicated at the last Status Conference, our intention is to prepare 89(F) Rule 89(F) packages or Rule 92 quater packages as it now will be in relation to every witnesses. The Prosecution has commenced it. We are about one-quarter of the way through. However, we do have some resource issues in that our legal resources are being deployed into trials which are immediately listed for trial or in trial, so it is slightly slower than we had anticipated. However, the Defence of course has all the information which will be in these packages, that is the statements of the witnesses, any exhibits, and the testimony in related cases. All we are doing is putting them into one package to make it easier for all parties in the court when we actually get to trial. We are not quite in the position to start handing them over, but once we're a little bit more further advanced, we can certainly disclose them with a view to seeking some sort of pre-trial agreement. But we would be doing that closer to trial when we have a better view of when the trial will be and the final witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, one thing depends on the other, doesn't it? We will address that issue of the hopefully soon possible start of the trial. But therefore, it would assist a lot if the Prosecution would focus on that issue. As to Rule 92 bis evidence, everything has been already said yesterday, I suppose. Are there any submissions here?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only thing which I would repeat so that it's in the Status Conference and on the public record is that the Prosecution's view, which we have expressed before, is that it's more appropriate to deal with who the 92 bis witnesses are immediately before trial or when a Trial Chamber has been assigned. The most recent difficulties in pre-trial Chambers making decisions have been in the Prlic case and the Seselj case where the Trial Chamber is now reviewing its original 92 bis decisions. So we very much want to be in the position that we have a Trial Chamber before we make the ultimate decision, which of course is the Trial Chamber's, and don't deploy resources in going down to take the statements in the former Yugoslavia, which is why we are preferring the 89(F) package from which a decision can be made in consultation with the Trial Chamber and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Thank you. Now to the agreed facts and adjudicated facts and stipulations on the indictment. First, as to the agreed facts. It was suggested several times by Defence counsel during the last two 65 ter conferences, and it is suggested now that the Prosecution act on Mr. Jovanovic's request regarding a proposal for an agreement on some basic issues such as the mentioned death certificates. Therefore, it is suggested that this will be now done before the next Status Conference. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That certainly is. The -- on the Trial Chamber's orders last year, we filed our proposed agreed facts. It was on the 8th of August last year, and Defence for Mr. Stanisic responded and has filed their counter-proposal. So there is something out there, but we'll certainly work on getting something more to the Defence before then. But of course the Defence could also, we suggest, respectfully, provide us with their own suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That indeed would help, wouldn't it? Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I suggest that it would be more effective if we look at this more closely when the Prosecution serve the revised pre-trial brief? There is much we potentially don't know about the Prosecution case so far, whether it's 1.000 exhibits from Serbia, potentially, whether it's the VRS archives and what's coming from them, whether it's a change to the way they put their case in the revised pre-trial brief, and I would be uncomfortable sitting down to agree finally, although there can be movement, I think there can be understandings reached through exchange of proposals which I think has happened thus far, but I would be uncomfortable with meeting any final agreement until we've reached the point of understanding precisely what constitutes the Prosecution case. We understand what the Prosecution's proposals are. We have looked at them and I can certainly suggest that as soon as we're in a position to know the Prosecution case we would work hard to reach agreements to expedite the final trial. That's our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Now, please, Mr. Jovanovic, what's your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is true that the Prosecution sent in a list of facts offered to the Defence for adoption and Mr. Stanisic's Defence responded to that, but I think that the evaluation made by Judge Kwon, the other Pre-Trial Judge, that it was an over-ambitious attempt on the part of the Prosecution, perhaps, and that to start off, we should concentrate on, if I can put it this way, less important facts, such as confirmation of death, autopsy reports and so on, so that we are expecting a reformulated proposal from the Prosecution to begin with. And then in a short -- that is something that we can respond to in a short space of time. Otherwise we fully agree with what my learned friend Mr. Jordash has just put forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. Now, I will turn to the adjudicated facts issue. As there are no Prosecution motions regarding these adjudicated facts, and there are references in Prosecution filings that there will be such requests, I might mention during yesterday's 65 ter conference with our Senior Legal Officer, Prosecution suggested it didn't want to bother the Trial Chamber with a motion on adjudicated facts. It made the analogy with 92 bis evidence on which maybe some Judges are reluctant to decide, as you referred to in this pre-trial phase, but the Chamber would like to invite Prosecution to file with the Court a proposal on adjudicated facts that -- the proposal that they submitted to the Defence in March 2006. Then the Defence can respond to this motion and the Court will want to rule on as many facts as it can during the pre-trial phase. Is that reasonable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It is certainly not unreasonable. As we explained in the Rule 65 ter conference yesterday, the Prosecution, on the 15th of March this year, forwarded a 47-page proposal on adjudicated facts with 288 suggested adjudicated facts to the Defence listing the source of the adjudicated fact and where it had been admitted in previous cases. I mean, the document is certainly in a file-able form. Before doing -- before filing it, we would wish to review the Simic and Brdjanin Appeals Chamber decisions which may be relevant. Simic is certainly relevant because there's an overlapping crime base in the Bosanski Samac crime base. When Your Honour a moment ago mentioned -- my submissions yesterday that we didn't want to bother the Trial Chamber, that's quite correct. Our view is I think burden is a better way of expressing it from our view-point that we took the view that it was better to do this inter partes and try and reach some sort of agreement before we came back to the Trial Chamber or Pre-Trial Chamber, because we didn't want to file something that was just waiting in cyberspace, so to speak, it being only of information for the Pre-Trial Chamber that we had exchanged suggestions for adjudicated facts with the difficulty that the Trial Chamber would not or may not consider itself bound by anything the Pre-Trial Chamber decides in relation to this. So that was the reason why we sent it by letter, but we're certainly happy to file it as information rather than, I would respectfully submit, a motion for a decision on adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly in regard to Mr. Re's suggestion that it's filed as information, then I would have no issue with that. As a motion, I would simply reiterate what I said a moment ago, which is that in terms of making sensible decisions the Defence are not in a position to, until we know what the Prosecution case is. But in terms of filing it as information, and I would have, as I say, no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yeah. This, of course, is true, I think. One cannot put the horse before the -- the cart before the horse, you know. I would again like to draw your attention to the decision of the Karemera Appeals Chamber which the Senior Legal Officer drew your attention to yesterday. The Appeals Chamber decision of the 16th of June, 2006. The reason to look at this decision is because it constitutes a turning point in the Appeals Chamber jurisprudence and as to the legal qualifications of facts. I also would like to draw your attention to what the Prlic Trial Chamber recently decided in this regard. The latest decision of -- on adjudicated facts of the Prlic Chamber of 7th of September, 2006. These are all means to streamline the case and to balance between the fairness and the expeditiousness of the trial and of the whole process, and therefore one has to do with the other. But I would like to address now as an extra point the anticipated length of this trial. The issue has been discussed yesterday at length, apparently. The Stanisic Defence believed that the position of the Prosecution that their case will take about six months was overly optimistic and the Chamber will take note of that position. Is there anything else the party would like to add, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just clarify what I was suggesting yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I understood that the six-month estimation was for the whole trial. That's what I was regarding as overly optimistic. Six months for the Prosecution case, that would appear to be certainly an estimate which I wouldn't disagree with and couldn't, as long as obviously sensible decisions are made about agreed facts and so on and so forth. So six months I don't have an issue with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I have to admit that I also first misunderstood it in the sense of six months for the overall duration of the trial, but it's important to note that this is referring only to the Prosecution case. Is that correct, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to make an estimate. When I say six months, it's a best guesstimate, really, but that depends so much on how many witnesses are called live, how much cross-examination there is, agreed facts, stipulations, adjudicated facts, the length of cross-examination, whether the accused testify, if so, for how long, how much evidence, if any, the Defence call. I would hope it could be done in six months, but it depends on so many factors that I can't -- I really can't say any better than that at the moment. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No. No. Thank you. Nothing to apologise. And I appreciate that -- I acknowledge that this is a difficult task. It's, according to my short experience now, it seems to be like an art, to streamline these cases and still be representative and fair at the same time. It's clear, whether we have limited resources, on the other hand, we have absolute commandments for fairness, and therefore I appreciate your efforts. Well, these efforts now will also have to do with the start of the trial. So may I ask the last point --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I meant to jump up. But I think I might have stolen my co-accused's jump up. There's still some confusion. We've now gone back to the issue of six months relating to the whole trial. Mr. Re just referred to the accused giving evidence, whether any Defence evidence is called and so on. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It was a little fuzzy, but I think, on the other hand, Mr. Re referred to the Prosecution case only.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would he say so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, your body language says something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It may be; it may be not. It depends on how many witnesses we can put on paper, whether the Defence is contesting the crime base. If the Defence isn't contesting the crime base, it will be much less. If it's a case concentrated on the linkage, and we call 20 witnesses, for example, it will take much less time. But if there's contest to the crime base, it will take longer. I just can't -- I can't give an estimate without some sort of agreement or focus on where the Defence is coming from. So six months could be the whole trial, or it could be the Prosecution case, depending upon that. But I don't think we're going to get an answer to that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Well, it's still not clear, and I think it would be better for the Prosecution to state its views as to how long their case will take, regardless of whether the Defence will conduct cross-examination or not, or what the accused's stand will be with respect to testimony or anything else. It would be a good idea if we had a realistic assessment, as far as that is possible, from the Prosecution about how long they intend to take in order to present their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I think that doesn't require any answer now. And we should now move to the trial preparations, the possible deadline to commence trial. During the last Status Conference, it was suggested that the Prosecution would need some four to six months for it to be ready to go to trial. This would mean the winter coming now, and yesterday at the 65 ter meeting, the Senior Legal Officer suggested that the Chamber will want to set up a work plan in order to be ready for trial in spring, around March, she said, of 2007. We have reviewed this position in light of clarifications of the Defence's oral submissions during yesterday's 65 ter conference. The Trial Chamber considers that the deadline should be extended, such that this case needs to be ready to go to trial around mid-summer 2007. I would say definitely before the summer recess and, if possible, early July 2007. The Trial Chamber will issue a written order regarding a work plan to be ready by that date in the next month, to be ready for that date in the next month. But before we do, we would like to once more hear observations of the parties in this respect. Would you like to make observations, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution, of course, will comply with any orders the Trial Chamber makes. Yesterday in the Rule 65 ter conference, I alerted the Defence and the Senior Legal Officer to the current work in progress of the Prosecution, I repeat it now for the public and the Status Conference. Since the last Status Conference, the Prosecution has, pursuant to high level agreements reached with the government of the Republic of Serbia, managed to view categories of documents within archives held by the Republic of Serbia. The agreement with the Republic of Serbia doesn't allow us to copy documents in situ, we have to request the documents where we have to first of all ask the archivist for the documents or to inspect ledgers to try and find them, and then take a note of the documents we want and then make a request for assistant from the Prosecutor's office to the government of Serbia. It's a different situation for the VRS and the government of Bosnia where we can take copies in the archive of whatever we wanted. Hence, the difference between the situation with the Serbian archives and the Bosnian archives. With the VRS, we will be in a position to disclose the material next month. I have reviewed the records. We have currently requested some 1500 or so documents based from the Republic of Serbia based upon our review of ledgers and spot samples of documents in their archives. The reason for the lateness of our doing this is it was not until earlier this year that the Prosecution was granted access in any way to these archives held by the Republic of Serbia, access to which had been the subject of litigation over at least four years in the case of Prosecutor against Slobodan Milosevic. After Mr. Milosevic's death, the Prosecutor has entered into an agreement with the Republic of Serbia allowing us finally to go to these archives and, as a result, it takes some time to organise access and to view them. We have made the requests, and we are awaiting receipt of these documents. We've also requested documents in the categories of ledgers which would lead us to further documents, but again, we have to await the Serbian government giving us those documents before we can actually request the further documents. That's the problem. So we simply ask the Trial Chamber to bear this in mind, the difficulties we faced in the Republic of Serbia's compliance under Article 29 and Rule 39 of the Statute and Rules, and the Prosecution's dilemma in balancing the rights of the accused and the rights of the international community in obtaining the evidence necessary. Once we have it, we hope it will focus the trial or focus the Prosecution and obviate the need to call oral evidence. We are very hopeful of that but we have to have the documents in house, and once we have them, it will take months, several months at least to review them, select those which we think are necessary, translate them and disclose them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That indeed is a complicated situation and understandable that it will take several months to structure these documents. How is the position of that Defence as to the start of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it would appear that everything depends upon this process, and with the best will in the world if the Prosecution obtain the documents in January, the Defence are not getting them until March or April, and it would take us a significant amount of time, if the documents run into hundreds, to be able to assess and work out their probative value, and from that work out what further investigations, if any, had to be undertaken, a process which, I would imagine, is going to be as long as the Prosecution's process of getting them and getting them to us. So whilst of course we would do everything to comply with any order to be ready by July 2007, on the face of it, putting aside Defence difficulties, it would appear to be quite a tight schedule. I would -- probably for Your Honour at this stage as well, the ill health of the accused and the fact that that slows the whole process down from the Defence preparation side of things. So it perhaps may be somewhat ambitious, given all of these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Of course it is ambitious, indeed, and will be tight. What is your view, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I agree with what my learned colleague has just said. The Defence will of course act in conformity with any ruling made by the Court. But with respect to the amount and volume of material that the Prosecution will be disclosing to the Defence, I think that the date that you mentioned, or, rather, July 2007 is a little over-ambitious, perhaps, as a deadline. But at all events, it will depend on how things proceed, how much material the Prosecution is going to disclose after it makes its selection, but I don't think this deadline would be sufficient for the Defence to analyse the documents whilst they have been disclosed and then to conduct its own investigations therein. So the Defence is not insisting upon a speedy trial, especially as the accused are on provisional release at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We have, of course, when discussing a tentative deadline, to take into account research on the side of the Defence. What do you think, Mr. Re? Let's speak of these documents you were just mentioning before. You would come across documents relevant to this case. I suppose you would include also exculpatory material, if you come across such material, or what would be your approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The broad categories of documents are things such as reports, intercepts, ledgers, information we just haven't been able to receive from the authorities in Serbia over the life-span of the Tribunal. We are, of course, looking for inculpatory material, but if we find exculpatory material under Rule 68 of course we will disclose it and disclose it as Rule 68 as we -- consistent with our obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. I mean before disclosing it, you would ask for that. You described the complicated procedure in Belgrade, and therefore, you can only disclose what you have in possession. Therefore, that was my question, if you would ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not quite -- can you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: How much efforts will be required then for the Defence to go and see what there is in supporting -- in support of their position and -- so therefore, I was asking myself: How would you behave? Like you find this and that, and you would then order it to be copied for you, and only then you would disclose it? It's a technical issue, but at the same time it's related to the question of the objectivity or not by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The procedure is different with, for example, the VRS archive searches and the Serbian ones. With the VRS, we collect the documents on the spot and mark whether we consider anything we find to be Rule 68 and then disclose it. So we can do it -- because we have the documents in our hand we can basically assess them at the time. With these documents, we have to request them, then receive them. Now if we see anything that we think is Rule 68 while in the archives, we also request that and provide that to the Defence. But we have to get it back -- and review it. So that adds to the procedure. So of course if we find anything in this -- in the process of searching, which we consider to be Rule 68, we will request it and ask the -- and provide it to the Defence. If that's the question Your Honour is asking me, that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you for this valuable clarification. Still it might require some effort, some investigative effort on the side of the Defence after having received these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's clear that the Prosecution are looking, as Mr. Re said, for inculpatory evidence. If they come across exculpatory, they'll seize it, but our approach, of course, will be completely the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Your approach would be more comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, we would look for obviously what was helpful. So it may be that we ourselves have to search the archives once the Prosecution are finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Of course. So let's agree on the tentative character of this potential deadline, and let's give it a try to come as close as possible to that goal. Do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. Nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So it's the question if there are any other matters which might be raised? Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I wanted to add just a point that in combination of all that issues, we will also have to view the possibilities of pre-trial briefs, then that will be included in the work plan, and we will set the dates as they same appropriate. So this brings us to the end of this Status Conference, and I would like to thank you, and also the interpreters again, of course, and everybody. And so we will schedule the next Status Conference as ruled -- as regulated in the rules. Thank you very much. ---Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at 12.49 p.m.
